content.text:
All 11 threads addressed and resolved; pushed as [d0bd46ed](https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/pull/467). CI is running.

## What I fixed (9 of 11)

**Three were real bugs**, and I'd call the middle one the most valuable catch of the batch:

- **Sender scalars escaped `Zeroizing`.** `generate_sender_key` copied out of the crypto crate's wipe-on-drop buffer into a bare `[u8; 32]`, which then moved through the fan-out and was dropped unwiped — on every send. That crate keeps key material in `Zeroizing` deliberately and my unwrap boundary silently undid it.
- **A configured instance with no master key answered `200 {"keys": []}`.** A client would pin an empty set, then fail to verify every notification it received, with only a server-side warning to explain it. Now a 503 — distinct from the 501 an un-opted-in instance returns, because the operator *has* opted in.
- **The admin revoke cleanup collapsed `Err` into "no handle" and deleted the row anyway**, destroying the only record of the handle. The relay kept a live route to a just-revoked device with nothing left for a retry to find.

Plus the CLI reporting bug: `retire`/`revoke` ran guarded UPDATEs and printed success regardless, so a mistyped `kid` read as a completed revocation while the real key stayed published. That one matters because an operator revoking a key believes they've just closed a compromise.

The rest were stale comments and docs — including the `notify-relay` dependency comment claiming "only `protocol` is exposed", which stopped being true the moment I made the relay a full library. That's mine, and it's exactly the kind of drift worth catching.

## What I declined

**The `push_handle IS NULL` guard.** There's one worker draining a FIFO mpsc, awaiting each job to completion, so handle writes land in registration order and the last is by construction newest. The proposed guard would *introduce* the bug: on two back-to-back re-registrations, job 2's write gets rejected because job 1's handle is already stored — stranding the handle for the superseded APNs token. I added a comment marking the FIFO ordering as load-bearing and replied on the thread with the reasoning.

I also kept the e2e's one-byte padding tolerance while taking the raw-bytes half of that suggestion. Base64's 4-chars-per-3-bytes step makes some bucket targets unreachable by any pad length; `plaintext_pad_len` documents and tests that. Removing the allowance would assert something the arithmetic never promised.

The queue-depth gauge is deferred to [MM-487](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-487/notify-expose-the-send-workers-queue-depth-as-a-metric) — legitimate, but it touches the metrics module, its name constants, and the operator docs table, and it carries a follow-on question about whether the queue should stay unbounded once observable.

Tests are up to 2264 (from 2261): the idempotency test now covers the revoke half it was named for, plus unknown-kid no-transition, admin-handle readability after revocation, and the new 503. Full workspace clippy `-D warnings`, tests, fmt, bruno and docs parity all green locally.

One caveat on CI: **CodeRabbit is running a fresh review round** on this commit and assertive bots reliably surface a new micro-nit after each fix batch. If it does, say the word and I'll triage the next round the same way rather than reflexively applying it.

One test is failing in CI with a 401 signature error even though it passes locally — looks like a classic intermittent issue. I'm suspecting the signature verification might be failing because of how the low-S canonical form is being enforced during verification, so I need to check my signing helper and how it's generating signatures.

That means roughly half of generated signatures end up with high-S values and get rejected by the verifier, which enforces low-S canonicalization. This would explain the flakiness — it's essentially a coin flip whether the test passes or fails on each run. The fact that it passes locally multiple times is suspicious for a true 50/50 scenario, so I should verify what the actual verification logic is doing and potentially run the test repeatedly to confirm the pattern.

The real fix is to normalize to low-S in my test helper to match what a real admin device would do, since the crypto documentation explicitly requires external signers to return low-S signatures themselves.

content.text:
**PDS gate passes.** Pushed as [f592f1a5](https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/pull/467).

## What was actually wrong

Not a regression in the feature — a bug in my test's signing helper.

ECDSA signatures are malleable: every signature has a high-S twin that verifies against the same key. The admin guard rejects the high-S form (matching `@atproto/crypto` and plc.directory strict verification, so one signature can't yield two valid requests). P-256's `SigningKey::sign` doesn't normalize, so my helper emitted a rejected signature whenever the nonce happened to land high.

That's a clean ~50/50 coin flip. Locally it passed the handful of times I ran it before pushing; CI lost the toss. When I ran it in a loop, **6 of 10 failed** — which is what turned "mysterious CI failure" into an obvious diagnosis.

The fix is the `normalize_s().unwrap_or(sig)` step that `admin_devices.rs`, `admin_list_accounts.rs`, and `admin_audit.rs` test helpers already carry; I wrote a fresh helper and omitted it. cd "$WT" && git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Never publish an empty sender-key set, whatever the cause

Follow-up on the earlier NoMasterKey fix, which closed one route to a silent
empty published set and left two open. `generate_sender_key`'s return value was
discarded, so a failed lazy generation fell through to `Ok(vec![])`; and if
every stored key fails to unwrap, the `filter_map` empties the set the same way.
Both end identically for a client: it pins nothing, then cannot verify a single
notification it receives.

Rather than guard each cause, `published_sender_keys` now enforces one invariant
at its exit — never return an empty set — so a future failure path is covered
the day it appears rather than the day someone notices. The new `NoUsableKey`
variant is distinct from `NoMasterKey` because the operator's fix differs: the
master key is present, so this is a generation failure or key material that no
longer decrypts under it (both already logged with their cause). Both map to
503; only the message differs.

Test covers the surviving path — a stored key wrapped under a previous KEK,
which is what a restored backup looks like. Verified it fails (200) without the
guard and passes (503) with it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git push 2>&1 | tail -2
